This is an attempt to understand the E-mailed comments to John Podesta about "Oversampling" Blacks, Indians, and older people by a Hillary consultant to John Podesta. This request happened during the 2008 Election Cycle and was specifically referencing "Atlas Polling".

http://www.zerohedge.com/news/2016-10-23/new-podesta-email-exposes-dem-playbook-rigging-polls-through-oversamples

https://americanlookout.com/tag/atlas-polling/

There seem to be two prevailing viewpoints on whether this comment was innocuous or evidence of an intention to manipulate the polling process to achieve a specific outcome.

The best evidence against the latter viewpoint is that this comment was probably relative to the idea that the intent of Tom Matzzie was to get good data in order to target campaign finances.

My argument here will be to the effect that both viewpoints are true.

"Oversampling" is a statistical term which means to effectively weight a subgroup within a data set higher to overcome some [usually environmental] problem with getting data relevant to your query when sampled subgroups are under-representative of the population. In the case of Election Polling it is probably because it is harder to get responses from members of this sub-group, but your analysts don't think they are any less in service to the larger data-collection effort.

So what it seems like Tom Matzzie is trying to do is find out where they are going to need to beef up polling efforts to get more responses.

However within the context Matzzie used "Oversampling" - the use of the term is incorrect. When a polling agency uses the term "Oversampling" they might mean calling more Blacks or Indians or old people than the proportions of other demographics. However in a purely scientific term, "Oversampling" is used as a mathematical weighting within an extant data set. So if the polling parlance were to be using the "technical" interpretation of the word "Oversampling" - it would mean they would call everyone they can possibly reach to try and get equivalent [proportional] demographic subgroups to respond and then use a formula to weight them the best way they can to simulate the reality of the data.

So here is where "Academics" and "Students of Human Nature" are already on slightly divergent paths. Because here, already, the "Politicians" and the "Scientists" are using the same word for two different things. Most of them don't realize the other is using the word differently, and so their arguments break down.

And there is a third group - people who see both the perspectives of the "Academic" and the "Scientist" - but also see the problem in terms of a time and energy/business equation.

When you pay over $450k to a company like Atlas - you are relying on their expertise to provide you with scientifically valid data which is meaningful. So immediately when someone like Tom Matzzie is openly broaching specific issues - which should be a normal part of the rigor of a scientific process; I become uneasy. Is Tom Matzzie "thinking out loud"? Is he just trying to show the rep at Atlas that he knows what he is talking about to set the bar for their interaction at the proper level? Or is Tom Matzzie broaching the subject of how Atlas can help them provide data which is useful to Tom Matzzie in a certain way?

Where the "Academic" fails is in having too much trust in both people and the scientific model.

Another thing a "business minded" person might consider is that, even if Matzzies comments are totally innocuous in some way - it shows his thinking that this is something he would bring up. Even if you had perfectly good and valid data to start your marketing plan - why would you start over again from scratch when you wanted to help use "Poling Momentum" to game the system later? You don't throw away data - and you don't use two different Polling Companies to collect the same data and prepare it into different products for your use.

So both viewpoints can be right, until both viewpoints need to rely on input from the opposing camp to find a greater truth.
